36.s: Which of the following is not true about the Anti-Defection Bill?
o: An MP or an MLA will be disqualified if he has voluntarily given up the membership of the party to which he belonged.
In the event of a member’s absence from voting in the House on a particular issue, an MP or MLA will be disqualified.
A member shall not be disqualified if there is a merger of political parties.
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha will not be disqualified if he becomes a member of another political party later on.
36.x: A presiding officer is protected only if he gives up party membership on election to the office and rejoins after demitting it; if he joins another party he is disqualified. Giving up membership, defying the whip (unless condoned in 15 days) and the merger exception are correctly stated.

36.s: If a party has 100 legislators (MLAs) in an assembly, as per anti-defection law, how many members are required to create a break-away faction without attracting disqualification?
o: None – no split is protected since 2003 (only a merger by 67 escapes)
36.src: APPSC Assistant Social, BC & Tribal Welfare Officers Screeni
36.x:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (None – no split is protected since 2003 (only a merger by 67 escapes)); it is added as option 5.
the one-third split exception (34 of 100) was deleted by the 91st Amendment, 2003 — now no split is protected; only a two-thirds merger (67 of 100) escapes (Rocket Polity #77)
Since the 91st Amendment (2003) deleted the one-third split exception, no break-away faction of any size escapes disqualification; only a merger backed by two-thirds (67 of 100) is protected. 34 (one-third) was the answer under the pre-2003 law, and 30, 33 and 35 were never right.

36.s: The merger of a political party with another political party in India is recognised in which of the following conditions?
o: When not less than one-third members of the
When not less than half members of the legislature
When not less than two-third members of the legisla-
When not less than three-fourth members of the leg-
36.x: Para 4: a merger is recognised when the original party merges with another and not less than two-thirds of its legislature party agree to it.

36.s: A member of State Legislature/Parliament is considered an exception of dis-qualification on the ground of defection in India, in which of the following condition?
o: If he voluntarily, gives up the membership of his
If he re-joins the political party after he ceases to hold
36.x: Para 5: a member elected presiding officer is not disqualified if he voluntarily gives up his party membership, or if he rejoins that party after he ceases to hold the office – both conditions are exceptions.

36.s: Under the Tenth Schedule of Indian constitution, a legislator will not be disqualified for defection if at least what fraction of the members of a party decide to merge with another party?
36.src: APPSC Assistant Statistical Officer & Other Posts General St
36.x: A legislator is not disqualified if two-thirds of the legislature party agree to merge the party with another (Para 4).

36.s: Which of the following statements is correct about the Anti-Defection Law?
o: The Anti-Defection Law protects members from disqualification in cases where one-third of the members of a legislative party split to form a new group.
A person disqualified on the grounds of defection can become a Minister if he belongs to the ruling party.

If a nominated member fails to join a political party within 6 months of commencement of his term, it is considered as grounds for disqualification of the member of a House of the State Legislature under the Tenth schedule of the constitution.
Disqualification on the grounds of defection does not apply when a member goes out of his party as a result of a merger of the party with another party.
36.src: APPSC Junior Assistant in Dr. NTR University of Health Scien
36.x: Disqualification does not apply when a member goes out of his party as a result of a merger (Para 4). The one-third split exception was deleted in 2003; a disqualified defector cannot become a Minister till re-elected (Art. 75(1B)/164(1B)); a nominated member is disqualified only if he joins a party after six months, not for failing to join.

36.s: Regarding the provisions related to disqualification on grounds of defection, choose the wrong answer
o: A member of the house belonging to any political party has voluntarily given up his membership of such party would be disqualified
Votes or abstain from voting in such house contrary to any direction issued by the political party to which he belongs would lead to disqualification
A nominated member of a House shall be disqualified for being a member of the house if he joins any political party after the expiration of six months from the date on which he takes his seat
If a party expel a legislator from the party, expelled member loses his seat in the house
36.src: APPSC Assistant Social, B.C. & Tribal Welfare Officers Mains
36.x: An expelled member does not lose his seat: he continues to belong to the party for Tenth Schedule purposes (G. Viswanathan 1996) and sits as unattached. Giving up membership, defying the whip and a nominated member joining a party after six months are grounds of disqualification.

36.s: Regarding anti defection, which of the following is not correct?
o: If a member defects from one party to some other party he is disqualified by the speaker
If a party expels an elected member of the party, the Member does not lose his seat in Legislature immediately
If a group of one-Third of members of the party decided to split, they will not lose their seats
If a group of 2/3 of the total members of a party decide to merge with some other party
36.src: APPSC Assistant Social, B.C. & Tribal Welfare Officers Mains
36.x: Since the 91st Amendment (2003) a one-third split no longer protects members, so that statement is not correct. A defector is disqualified by the Speaker, an expelled member keeps his seat, and a two-thirds merger is protected.

36.s:
Assertion (A): An MP or MLA may be treated as having voluntarily given up party membership even without formally resigning.
Reason (R): Conduct such as publicly campaigning for an opposition party can constitute voluntarily giving up membership.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
36.x: Both are true: a member can be held to have given up party membership without resigning, because conduct such as campaigning for a rival party counts. R explains A.
36.tq: Recall that conduct can amount to giving up membership.
n: Voluntarily giving up party membership is broader than formal resignation and includes conduct. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
An MP or MLA can be considered to have voluntarily given up party membership by publicly campaigning for an opposition party. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
An MP or MLA can be considered to have voluntarily given up party membership without submitting a formal resignation letter. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
"**Voluntarily giving up membership**" is **broader** than **formal resignation** — it can be inferred from **conduct**.
**Publicly campaigning** for an **opposition party**, even without a resignation letter, counts — which explains A.
xa: **Ravi S. Naik v UoI (1994)**: voluntarily giving up membership is **not the same as resigning**.
**G. Viswanathan (1996)**: an **expelled** member **still belongs** to his party; joining another party = giving up membership.
Other ground: **voting or abstaining contrary to the party whip** without **prior permission** (**Para 2(1)(b)**).

36.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding a Presiding Officer under the Anti-Defection Law?
o: A Presiding Officer cannot rejoin the original party after demitting office.
A Presiding Officer may face disqualification for joining another political party after vacating office.
A Presiding Officer may face disqualification for joining another political party while holding office.
A Presiding Officer can voluntarily give up party membership upon election to the Chair.
36.x: Option A is incorrect: a presiding officer may give up party membership on election to the Chair and rejoin the party after leaving office. Joining another party, during or after the term, disqualifies them.
36.tq: Discriminate rejoining the original party from joining another.
n: A presiding officer is disqualified for joining another political party while holding office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer is disqualified for joining another political party after vacating office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer may voluntarily give up party membership upon election to the Chair. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer may rejoin the original party after demitting office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xs: The incorrect statement is that a **Presiding Officer cannot rejoin the original party after demitting office** — so option **(1)** is the answer.
A Presiding Officer **may voluntarily give up** party membership on **election to the Chair** and **rejoin** the original party after demitting office.
He is disqualified only for **joining another political party** while holding office or after vacating it — so options (2), (3), (4) are true.
xa: This exception is **Para 5**, covering **Speaker/Deputy Speaker/Chairman/Deputy Chairman**; it is **in force**.
Criticism: Indian Speakers **do not resign from their party**, so they are seen as partisan.
The Presiding Officer decides defection petitions under **Para 6**.

36.s:
Consider the following statements about the grounds of disqualification under the Tenth Schedule:
1. A member who votes against the party whip without prior permission is not disqualified if the party condones it within 30 days.
2. An independent member is disqualified if he joins any political party after his election.
3. A nominated member who joins a political party within six months of taking his seat is not disqualified.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
36.x: Statement 1 is the incorrect one: the party must condone the vote within 15 days (Para 2(1)(b)), not 30. Statements 2 and 3 are correct – an independent is disqualified on joining a party; a nominated member may join a party within six months.

36.s:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).
Assertion (A): A merger of a legislator's original party with another party saves him from disqualification only if not less than two-thirds of the legislature party agree to it.
Reason (R): The 91st Amendment (2003) deleted the one-third split exception of Paragraph 3.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
36.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the two-thirds merger rule is Para 4, which remains in force, while R is about the separate split exception (Para 3) that was deleted in 2003.

36.s:
Consider the following statements about the criticism of the anti-defection law:
1. It is said to stifle intra-party dissent and the free expression of legislators.
2. The two-thirds merger route has been criticised as a way to defend mass defection.
3. It prohibits en-bloc (bulk) defections carried out through a merger.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
36.x: Statement 3 is wrong: the law 'banned retail defections and legalised wholesale defections' – en-bloc defection through a merger is not covered. Statements 1 and 2 are the standard criticisms.

36.s: Regarding the privileges of the parliament, choose the wrong answer?
o: Constitution guaranteed freedom of speech in parliament
The Members of parliament are immune from arrest in Civil cases whether the parliament is in session or not.
In Criminal cases parliament members cannot be arrested while they are in the House in Session
Parliament has freedom to publish its proceedings
36.src: APPSC Assistant Social, B.C. & Tribal Welfare Officers Mains
36.x: Freedom from arrest applies only in civil cases and only during a session and 40 days before and after it, not 'whether Parliament is in session or not'. Free speech (Art. 105(1)), the right to publish proceedings and the rule that no member is arrested within the precincts without the presiding officer's permission are all correct.

36.s: Which of the following punishments can be awarded by the Lok Sabha to a member held guilty of breach of privileges or contempt of the House?
o: Expulsion from the House and thereby declaring his seat as vacant
36.x: A House punishes members and outsiders by reprimand, admonition or imprisonment, and members also by suspension or expulsion (Raja Ram Pal 2007 upheld expulsion). It does not impose fines, and imprisonment lasts only till the session ends, so 'six months' is wrong.

36.s: Which of the following punishments can the Lok Sabha impose on members who behave in breach of privilege or contempt of the House?
o: Expelling from the House and declaring the seat vacant
36.x: A House punishes by reprimand, admonition or imprisonment, and members also by suspension or expulsion. It does not impose fines, and imprisonment cannot outlast the session, so expulsion with the seat declared vacant is the valid option.

36.s: Which of the following statement is correct regarding Parliamentary Privileges?
o: Parliamentary Privileges are the privileges tha are enjoyed collectively by each House of the Parliament, and not by the Members individually
Only Members can be punished for contempt by reprimand and admonition but not outsiders
The phrase 'Breach of Privilege' has wider implications than the 'Contempt of the House
The Members cannot be arrested during the session of Parliament but this privilege is available only in civil cases and not in criminal cases or preventive detention cases
36.x: Members cannot be arrested during a session and 40 days before and after it, but only in civil cases, not criminal or preventive detention cases. Privileges are both collective and individual, outsiders can be punished too, and contempt is wider than breach of privilege.

36.s: All following statements regarding the privileges of Parliament members are correct except
36.x: Members' individual privileges include freedom of speech, freedom from arrest in civil cases and freedom from attendance as a witness while the House sits. Privileges are also collective (of each House), so 'only individual freedom' is the incorrect statement.

36.s: Under which Article of the Constitution the Courts have been prohibited from inquiring the proceedings of the Parliament?
36.x: Article 122 bars courts from inquiring into the validity of proceedings of Parliament on the ground of irregularity of procedure (Art. 212 for States).

36.s: The powers, privileges and immunities of either House of Parliament and of its Committee and Members have mainly be laid down in Article ……… of the Constitution of India.
36.x: Article 105 (Art. 194 for State Legislatures) lays down the powers, privileges and immunities of each House of Parliament, its members and committees.

36.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 75(1A) — Fifteen per cent limit on the Union Council of Ministers
Para 3 of the Tenth Schedule — Split exception
Para 4 of the Tenth Schedule — Merger exception
Article 105(1)-(2) — Fifteen per cent limit on a State Council of Ministers
36.x: Article 105(1)-(2) concerns freedom of speech and related parliamentary privileges. The 15 per cent limit on a State Council of Ministers is provided under Article 164(1A).
36.tq: Find the wrong authority-provision pairing by separating privilege provisions from ministerial-limit provisions.
xs: **Article 105(1)-(2)** is wrongly paired: it is about **freedom of speech / privileges** — option **(4)**.
The **15%** cap on a **State** Council of Ministers is **Art. 164(1A)**.
The other pairs are correct: **Art. 75(1A)** = Union **15%** cap; **Para 3** = split; **Para 4** = merger.
xa: **Art. 164(1A)** sets a minimum of **12** ministers.
**Arts 75(1B), 164(1B), 361B** bar a disqualified defector from ministerial/remunerative posts.
All came via the **91st Amendment, 2003**.

36.s: Which Article bars courts from questioning proceedings of Parliament on the ground of procedural irregularity?
36.x: Article 122 protects proceedings of Parliament from court inquiry for procedural irregularity; Article 212 does the same for State Legislatures.

36.s: Which of the following is NOT an individual privilege of a Member of Parliament?
o: Freedom of speech in the House
Freedom from arrest in civil cases during a session
Right to exclude strangers from the sittings of the House
36.x: Excluding strangers from its sittings is a collective privilege of the House; the others are privileges of individual members.

36.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Provision)
A. Article 105
B. Article 194
C. Article 122
D. Lok Sabha Rule 222
List-II (Subject)
i. Powers and privileges of the State Legislatures and their members
ii. Notice by a member raising a question of breach of privilege
iii. Courts not to inquire into proceedings of Parliament for irregularity of procedure
iv. Powers and privileges of the Houses of Parliament and their members
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
36.x: Art. 105 – Parliament's privileges; Art. 194 – State Legislatures'; Art. 122 (and 212 for States) – courts cannot question proceedings for irregularity of procedure; LS Rule 222 (RS Rule 187) – notice of breach of privilege.

36.s:
Consider the following statements about parliamentary privileges:
1. They are codified in a single statute enacted by Parliament.
2. In a breach of privilege case the final decision is taken by the House.
3. The Committee of Privileges of the Rajya Sabha has 15 members and is chaired by the Chairman.
4. The Committee of Privileges of the Lok Sabha has 15 members nominated by the Speaker.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
36.x: Statements 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 1 is wrong – privileges are not codified; they rest on the Constitution, conventions, rules, statutes and court rulings. Statement 3 is wrong – the Rajya Sabha committee has 10 members and is usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman.

36.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Members of Parliament enjoy freedom from arrest in civil cases during a session and 40 days before and after it.
2. The right to receive immediate information of the arrest of a member is an individual privilege of that member.
3. A House can punish both its members and outsiders for breach of privilege or contempt.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
36.x: Statement 2 is wrong: receiving immediate information of a member's arrest, detention, conviction or release is a collective privilege of the House. Statements 1 and 3 are correct – arrest immunity is civil only (not criminal or preventive detention).

36.s:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).
Assertion (A): A House of Parliament can impose a fine on a person found guilty of contempt of the House.
Reason (R): Contempt of the House is wider than breach of privilege.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
36.x: A is false: the punishments are reprimand, admonition, imprisonment (till the session ends) and, for members, suspension or expulsion – no fine. R is true: every breach is a contempt, but not every contempt is a breach of a specific privilege.

36.s:
Consider the following statements about court rulings on legislative privilege:
1. In Raja Ram Pal (2007) the Supreme Court upheld the expulsion of members by the House.
2. In Sita Soren (2024) a five-judge Bench held that legislators have no immunity for bribery connected with a speech or vote.
3. Sita Soren overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
36.x: Statement 2 is wrong: Sita Soren was decided by a seven-judge Bench. Statements 1 and 3 are correct – Raja Ram Pal upheld expulsion (privilege decisions reviewable only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality), and Sita Soren overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao.

36.s: On any issue pertaining to the disqualification of any member of Lok Sabha under 10th Schedule of Indian Constitution, the final decision is taken by ……… .
36.x: Para 6: the Speaker decides defection disqualification of a Lok Sabha member, acting as a tribunal (subject to judicial review, Kihoto 1992). The President and the ECI have no role.

36.s:
Consider the following statements :
I. If any question arises as to whether a Member of the House of the People has become subject to disqualification under the 10th Schedule, the President's decision in accordance with the opinion of the Council of Union Ministers shall be final.
II. There is no mention of the word 'political party' in the Constitution of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
36.x: I is wrong: Tenth Schedule questions are decided by the Speaker (Lok Sabha), not the President on the Council's advice. II is wrong: the term 'political party' appears in the Tenth Schedule.

36.s: Where the question which has arisen is as to whether the Speaker of a House has become subject to disqualification under 10th schedule, the question shall be referred for the decision of
o: Such member of the house as the house may elect in this behalf
None of the given answers is correct
36.src: APPSC Assistant Social, B.C. & Tribal Welfare Officers Mains
36.x: Tenth Schedule para 6(1): where the question is whether the Chairman or Speaker is disqualified, it is decided by such member of the House as the House may elect.

36.s: In July 2026, what did the Bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe say about the shortcomings of Paragraph 4?
o: Outside the jurisdiction of every constitutional authority
Matters for the Election Commission alone
36.x: The Bench sought the Centre’s reply but observed that any shortcomings in Paragraph 4 were matters for Parliament.
36.tq: Distinguish a judicial observation about legislative remedy from a transfer of jurisdiction.
xs: The Bench said any shortcomings are **"matters for Parliament"** — option **(1)**.
**Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe** sought the **Centre's reply** on a plea against "**deemed merger**" under **Para 4**.
xa: **Subhash Desai (2023)**: two-thirds of legislators cannot by themselves create a **deemed merger**.
Para 4 has **two tests**: the **original political party** must merge and **two-thirds** of the legislature party must agree.
Timeline: Telangana contempt warning (Feb **2026**) → AAP and TMC "merger" cases (Apr-Jul **2026**).

36.s: In the Karnataka defection case (2019), the Supreme Court upheld the disqualification of how many rebel MLAs?
36.x: The Court upheld the disqualification of 17 rebel MLAs but held the Speaker could not bar them from contesting till the end of the term.
xa: **Karnataka 2019** is also an example of the **resignation route**.
**Telangana**: SC gave the Speaker a **final 3 weeks** (Feb **2026**).
Speaker decisions reviewable for **mala fides**, **perversity**, violation of **natural justice**.

36.s: In Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur, with what did the Supreme Court ask Parliament to consider replacing the Speaker in defection cases?
36.x: The Court suggested a permanent independent tribunal; it did not transfer Tenth Schedule decisions to the Election Commission.

36.s: In the Telangana Speaker matter, how much time did the Supreme Court later allow for deciding the last two of ten BRS disqualification petitions?
36.x: After a time-bound direction, the Supreme Court gave three weeks for the last two of ten BRS petitions, warning of contempt.
xa: The **10 BRS MLAs** had moved to **Congress**.
**Keisham (2020)**: **three months** limit.
AP precedent: **23 YSRCP MLAs** (2014-19), petitions **never decided**.

36.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Subhash Desai judgment (May 2023)?
o: The political party appoints the whip
The political party appoints the leader in the House
Legislators alone can bring about a 'deemed merger'
The legislature party does not override the political party
36.x: Subhash Desai held that the political party, not the legislature party, appoints the whip and leader, and that legislators alone cannot create a deemed merger.

36.s: In the Karnataka defection case (2019), what did the Supreme Court hold that the Speaker cannot do?
o: Disqualify rebels for giving up membership
Bar the disqualified MLAs from contesting elections
36.x: The Court upheld the disqualification of 17 rebels but held that the Speaker cannot bar them from contesting.

36.s:
Consider the following statements about the disqualification of legislators:
1. A question of general (non-defection) disqualification of an MP is decided by the President on the binding opinion of the Election Commission.
2. A defection question under the Tenth Schedule is decided by the Speaker or Chairman acting as a tribunal.
3. The Speaker must obtain the opinion of the Election Commission before deciding a defection case.
4. Article 191 deals with the disqualifications for membership of a State Legislature.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
36.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the ECI is not consulted in defection cases – its binding opinion applies only to general disqualification decided by the President/Governor (Arts 103, 192).

36.s:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).
Assertion (A): Presiding officers have often delayed deciding defection petitions.
Reason (R): The Tenth Schedule prescribes no time limit for the presiding officer to decide a defection petition.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
36.x: Both are true and R explains A: the Schedule sets no time limit, and Speakers remain members of their parties – hence the delays (the SC in Keisham 2020 later asked for decisions ordinarily within three months).

36.s:
With reference to Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), consider the following statements:
1. The Supreme Court upheld the validity of the Tenth Schedule by a 3:2 majority.
2. Paragraph 7 was struck down because it had not been ratified by the States under Article 368(2).
3. Judicial review of a Speaker's decision is available even before the decision is made.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
36.x: Statement 3 is wrong: judicial review is available only after the decision, on limited grounds such as mala fides, perversity or violation of natural justice. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

36.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Case)
A. Ravi S. Naik (1994)
B. G. Viswanathan (1996)
C. Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020)
D. Subhash Desai (2023)
List-II (Holding)
i. The political party, not the legislature party, appoints the whip
ii. An expelled member still belongs to his party
iii. Giving up party membership can be inferred from conduct
iv. Disqualification petitions to be decided ordinarily within three months
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
36.x: Ravi S. Naik – voluntarily giving up membership ≠ resigning, inferred from conduct; G. Viswanathan – expelled member still belongs to the party; Keisham – three months; Subhash Desai – the political party appoints the whip and leader.

36.s: As seen from the experience, the anti defection law in India could achieve the following?
o: Large number of disqualifications of legislators
Resulted only in additional powers to presiding officers of legislatures
36.x: The paper's key: in practice the law has not stopped defections (mass 'mergers', resignations) and its main result has been to make presiding officers the deciders of defection cases, often criticised for partisan delay. Disqualifications have been few.

36.s: What does 'resort politics' refer to in the context of anti-defection and floor tests?
o: Sending legislators abroad for parliamentary training
Dissolving the legislature before a confidence motion
Sequestering legislators before a floor test to prevent poaching
Suspending legislators who abstain from voting
36.x: Resort politics involves keeping legislators together or sequestered before a floor test to prevent rival parties from poaching them.
36.tq: Decode the political practice from its purpose rather than from its literal name.
xs: Resort politics = **sequestering legislators before a floor test** to stop **poaching** — option **(3)**.
It is one of the **ways around the law**, along with the **resignation route** and **merger misuse**.
xa: **Resignation route**: MLAs **resign** to cut the majority mark (Karnataka **2019**, MP **2020**).
**Merger misuse**: Para 4 **two-thirds** rule as a defence for mass defection.
**AAP**: **7 of 10** Rajya Sabha MPs claimed a "merger" with the BJP (Apr **2026**).

36.s: What do legislators do in the 'resignation route' used to avoid disqualification proceedings?
o: Seek prior permission from the Election Commission before switching parties
Resign, lowering the majority mark, and later re-contest on the new party's ticket
Abstain from every vote until the next election
Merge into the new party without resigning
36.x: In the resignation route, MLAs resign instead of defecting, reducing the majority mark without disqualification, and may re-contest on the new party's ticket.
xa: Examples: **Karnataka 2019**, **MP 2020**.
**Karnataka 2019**: SC upheld disqualification of **17** rebel MLAs.
**Resort politics**: legislators **sequestered** before a floor test.

36.s: Which of the following is a newer proposal concerning the anti-defection law?
o: Exempting independent members from the law
Fixed timelines for Speakers and an independent tribunal
36.x: Newer proposals include fixed constitutional timelines for Speakers and an independent tribunal, the latter suggested for consideration by the Supreme Court in 2020.
xa: **Keisham (2020)**: decide within **three months**.
Reform: limit whips to **confidence votes and Money Bills**.
**Telangana**: SC gave a **final 3 weeks** with a **contempt** warning (Feb **2026**).

36.s: What does the proposal to limit the whip and disqualification under the anti-defection law to confidence and money votes seek to ensure for legislators?
o: Vote against every money bill without party discipline
Avoid all party whips during the entire legislative term
Dissent even on a confidence motion without consequences
Dissent freely on matters that do not threaten the government's survival
36.x: The proposal would retain party discipline for votes threatening government survival, such as confidence, no-confidence and money bills, while allowing dissent on other matters.
36.tq: Apply the reform principle to distinguish survival votes from ordinary legislative votes.
xs: Legislators could **dissent freely on votes that do not threaten the government's survival** — option **(4)**.
The whip would apply only to **confidence and no-confidence motions and money bills**.
So discipline stays on confidence and money votes — options (1), (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: Backers: **Dinesh Goswami (1990)** and **Law Commission (1999)**.
**Manish Tewari's private member's Bill (2010)** proposed the same.
Criticism it answers: the law **muzzles dissent** without stopping mass defections.

36.s:
Arrange the following reform proposals in chronological order:
A. Law Commission’s 170th Report
B. Dinesh Goswami Committee recommendation
C. Manish Tewari’s private member’s Bill
D. Supreme Court suggestion to consider an independent tribunal
36.x: The sequence is Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990), Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999), Manish Tewari’s Bill (2010), and the Supreme Court’s independent-tribunal suggestion (2020).
36.tq: Fix the earliest and latest items first, then place the intermediate proposals by year.
xs: Correct order: **B, A, C, D** — option **(1)**.

44.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the High Court’s power of superintendence?

44.x: Option B is incorrect: under Article 227(4), superintendence does not cover courts and tribunals set up under Armed Forces laws. It does cover all other courts and tribunals in the High Court's territory, judicially and administratively.
44.tq: Recall the Armed Forces exception in Article 227.
n: Article 227 gives High Courts power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
A High Court exercises administrative superintendence over subordinate courts and tribunals throughout its territorial jurisdiction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
A High Court exercises judicial superintendence over subordinate courts and tribunals throughout its territorial jurisdiction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
High Court superintendence does not extend to courts and tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Armed Forces exception to High Court superintendence is provided by Article 227(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xs: The incorrect statement is that superintendence **extends to courts and tribunals under laws relating to the Armed Forces** — so option **(2)** is the answer.
**Article 227(4)** excludes **military tribunals**.
Art. 227 gives **administrative and judicial superintendence** over all subordinate **courts and tribunals** in its territory — so (1), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: It is **revisional** and can be exercised **suo motu**.
⚠ The SC has **no** Art. 227-type power.
Similarly, SC's **Art. 136(2)** SLP does not lie against **Armed Forces Courts**.

44.x: Both are true: High Courts' writ power under Article 226 is discretionary, and Article 32 is a fundamental right. A fact about Article 32 cannot explain Article 226, so R does not explain A.
44.tq: Ask whether a fact about Article 32 explains Article 226.
n: The writ power of a High Court is discretionary. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — so option **(2)** is correct.
A: the HC's writ power under **Article 226** is **discretionary**.
R: **Article 32** is itself a **Fundamental Right** — a fact about the SC's remedy, not why Art. 226 is discretionary.
xa: Art. 226 covers FRs **and other legal rights** — **wider than Art. 32**.
Writs may be refused where an **effective alternative remedy** exists.
An HC can issue writs beyond its territory if the **cause of action** arises within.

46.s: The distribution of legislative subjects among the Union, State and Concurrent Lists of the Seventh Schedule operates through which Article?
46.x: Article 246 gives effect to the three Lists of the Seventh Schedule. Article 245 deals with the territorial extent of laws, Article 248 with residuary powers, and Article 254 with repugnancy.
xs: The Seventh Schedule's three lists operate through **Article 246** — option **(2)**.
**Article 248** is the **residuary powers** Article (Part XI, Chapter I).
Precedence under it: **Union > Concurrent > State**.
xa: Three lists: **I - Union**, **II - State**, **III - Concurrent**.

50.s: Which of the following tax is collected by Gram Panchayat ?
50.src: AP Grama Ward Sachivalayam Ward Welfare & Development Secret
50.x: A Gram Panchayat levies taxes and fees such as house tax and the tax on fairs and markets (fair tax), as authorised by State law under Art. 243H. Sales tax was a State tax and customs and excise are Union taxes.

50.s: Under which Article of the Constitution of India are taxes levied and collected by the centre and assigned to the states?
50.x: Under Article 269 taxes on inter-State sale and consignment of goods are levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the States. Art. 268A (service tax) was omitted, 270 is the shared pool and 271 surcharges.

50.s:
Consider the following statements in connection with the distribution of tax revenues between the Centre and the States:

I. The proceeds of the surcharges levied on taxes and duties referred to in Article 269 and Article 270 of the Constitution of India, would be shared between the Centre and the States.

II. Article 268A and Article 272 of the Constitution of India were both repealed by same Constitutional Amendment Act.

III. Tax on the sale of petroleum crude is levied by the Centre but collected by the States.

IV. The net proceeds of tax categories that are falling under Article 269 of the Constitution of India, do not form a part of the Consolidated Fund of India.
Which of the above statement/statements is/are valid?
50.x: Only IV is valid: Art. 269 proceeds do not form part of the CFI. I is wrong because Art. 271 surcharges go wholly to the Union; II is wrong because Art. 272 was omitted by the 80th Amendment (2000) and 268A by the 101st (2016); III is wrong because tax on the sale of petroleum crude is levied by the States (State List).

50.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the levying, collecting and distribution of Income Tax is correct?
o: The Union levies, collects and distributes the proceeds of income tax between itself and the States
The Union levies, collects and keeps all the proceeds of income tax to itself
The Union levies and collects the tax but all the proceeds are distributed among the States
Only the surcharge levied on income tax is shared between the Union and the States
50.x: Income tax (other than on agricultural income) is levied and collected by the Union and its net proceeds are distributed between the Union and the States under Art. 270 on the Finance Commission's advice; only the surcharge stays with the Union.

50.s: Under which Article of the Constitution of India, Taxes are levied and collected by the centre but distributed between the centre and the States?
50.x: Article 270 covers taxes levied and collected by the Union and distributed between the Union and the States. Art. 268 taxes are collected by the States, 269 taxes are assigned to the States and 271 surcharges are kept by the Union.

50.s: In India non-agricultural income tax is
o: levied by the Centre and fully distributed among the States.
levied and appropriated by the Centre.
levied by the Centre and shared with the States.
50.x: Non-agricultural income tax is levied by the Centre and shared with the States (Art. 270 divisible pool). It is not kept wholly by the Centre, nor given wholly to the States; only agricultural income tax is a State tax.

50.s: Excise tax on liquor is levied by
50.x: Excise duty on alcoholic liquor for human consumption is a State List subject (Entry 51), levied and retained by the State Government.

50.s: Which of the following tax is levied by Union and collected and appropriated by States?
50.x: Under Art. 268 stamp duties on bills of exchange, cheques, insurance policies etc. are levied by the Union but collected and appropriated by the States. Estate duty and taxes on newspapers were old Art. 269 items (now Art. 270 / GST).

50.s:
Consider the following statements- In India taxes on transactions in Stock-Exchanges and Futures Markets are –
1. Levied by Union.
2. Collected by the State Government.
50.x: Taxes (other than stamp duty) on stock-exchange and futures-market transactions are Union List Entry 90 – levied and collected by the Union (old Art. 269, now the Art. 270 pool). They are not collected by the States, so only statement 1 is correct.

50.s: Under constitutional provision of tax assignment in India, which of the following is a tax exclusively imposed and collected by the states?
50.x: Land revenue (State List Entry 45) is imposed and collected exclusively by the States. Income tax and corporation tax are Union taxes and GST is shared.

50.s: Which of the following is levied and collected by the Centre, but assigned to the States?
50.x:
Most books and keys: taxes on railway fares (original Art. 269). Strictly, since the 80th Amendment (2000) railway-fare taxes are in the Art. 270 pool; today Art. 269 covers only taxes on inter-State sale and consignment of goods.
the 80th Amendment (2000) moved railway-fare taxes from Art. 269 into the Art. 270 divisible pool — now Art. 269 assigns to the States only taxes on inter-State sale/purchase and consignment of goods (Laxmikanth Ch15).
Taxes on railway fares and freights were levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the States under the original Art. 269 – the textbook answer. Customs and income tax are shared Union taxes and stamp duty is collected by the States.

50.s: Agriculture Income Tax is assigned to the State Government by-
50.x: Tax on agricultural income is assigned to the States by the Constitution itself (State List Entry 46). The Finance Commission, NDC and Inter-State Council cannot assign taxes.

50.s: Excise duty obtained on alcoholic medicines used by people is a source of revenue for whom?
o: Source of revenue of the Centre
Source of revenue of the States
Source of revenue of the Union Territories
Source of revenue of both the Central and State governments
50.x:
the 101st Amendment (2016) removed excise on medicinal and toilet preparations from Art. 268 — now such preparations are taxed under GST (CGST + SGST) (Laxmikanth Ch15 p.231).
Before GST, excise on medicinal and toilet preparations containing alcohol was levied by the Union but collected and kept by the States (Art. 268), so it was State revenue (now, under GST, not an Art. 268 duty).

50.s: Under which of the following taxes the total amount payable by an individual is limited by the Constitution?
o: Tax on profession, trade, and callings
50.x: Art. 276(2) caps the total tax on professions, trades, callings and employments payable by any person at ₹2,500 a year – the only such ceiling in the Constitution.

50.s: Which one of the following taxes is imposed and charged by the Union, but is divided into Union and the States?
o: Taxes on items except for agriculture income
Taxes on railway fares and freights
50.x:
Printed key: Customs. Strictly, since the 80th Amendment (2000, from 1996) corporation tax and customs are also in the Art. 270 pool; income tax is the classic answer and the only one that fits under the Constitution before 1996.
'Taxes on income other than agricultural income' is the tax the Union levies and collects but shares with the States (Art. 270) – the only one shared under the original Constitution. Railway-fare taxes were assigned wholly to the States, and corporation tax and customs became shareable only with the 80th Amendment.

50.s: As per present laws, which of the following can levy tax on agriculture?
o: Neither Union nor State can levy tax
50.src: APPSC Hostel Welfare Officer Grade-II Screening Test 2017
50.x: Tax on agricultural income is State List Entry 46, so only the States can levy it; the Union's income tax excludes agricultural income.

50.s:
Consider the following statements about the distribution of tax revenues:
1. The net proceeds of taxes under Article 269 that are assigned to the States do not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.
2. IGST on inter-State supplies under Article 269A is shared as Parliament provides on the advice of the GST Council.
3. Article 268A on service tax was omitted by the 101st Amendment, 2016.
4. The divisible pool under Article 270 includes surcharges and cesses levied by the Union.
How many of the above statements are correct?
50.x: Statement 4 is incorrect – Art. 270 covers Union taxes EXCEPT the 268, 269 and 269A taxes, surcharges (Art. 271) and cesses. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct as per the notes.

50.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Corporation tax became shareable with the States only from 1996, under the 80th Amendment.
2. The 80th Amendment folded surcharges on Union taxes into the Article 270 pool.
3. Before 2000, taxes on railway fares and freights were levied and collected by the Union but assigned to the States.
How many of the above statements are correct?
50.x: Statement 2 is incorrect – surcharges (Art. 271) remain with the Union alone; the 80th Amendment moved the old Art. 269 assigned taxes into the pool. Statements 1 and 3 are correct as per the notes.

50.s:
Consider the following statements about taxes in the State domain:
1. Land revenue, agricultural income tax, State excise on alcoholic liquor and taxes on vehicles are all levied by the States.
2. Taxes on the sale of petrol, diesel and ATF, which are outside GST, are levied by the Centre.
3. Article 276 empowers the States to levy a tax on professions, trades, callings and employments.
4. The Constitution caps the total profession tax payable by a person at ₹250 a year.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
50.x: Statement 2 is incorrect – taxes on the sale of petroleum crude, diesel, petrol, natural gas, ATF and liquor are levied by the STATES. Statement 4 is incorrect – the cap is ₹2,500 a year; ₹250 applied only till the 60th Amendment, 1988. Statements 1 and 3 are correct as per the notes.

50.s: Which authority has the power to recommend the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States?
o: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
50.src: APPSC Assistant Tribal Welfare Officer (A.P. Tribal Welfare
50.x: The Finance Commission (Art. 280) recommends how the net proceeds of shareable taxes are divided between the Union and the States. The CAG only certifies the net proceeds; the GST Council advises on GST, not on the divisible pool.

50.s: Which one of the following authorities recommends the principles governing the grants‑in‑aid of the revenues to the states out of the Consolidated Fund of India?
50.x: Under Art. 280(3)(b) the Finance Commission recommends the principles governing grants-in-aid to States out of the CFI. The Inter-State Council, Finance Ministry and PAC have no such constitutional role.

50.s: The financial resource between Centre and State is distributed on
50.x: The sharing of tax revenue between the Centre and States (Arts 270, 275) follows the Finance Commission's recommendations under Art. 280, not those of the Finance Ministry, RBI or NABARD.

50.s: Inter se distribution of tax shares, by the Finance Commission, amongst the states is known as:
50.src: APPSC Assistant Director of Economics, Assistant Commissione
50.x: The Finance Commission's division of the divisible pool between the Centre and the States is vertical devolution; the inter se distribution among the States is horizontal distribution (Art. 280(3)(a)).

50.s: Compositional shift from grants to tax devolution from Centre to State causes
o: additional fiscal burden on the Centre
increase in share of unconditional transfers to States
demand from States to increase tax rates
lack of fiscal space to carry out specific purpose transfer to States
50.x: Tax devolution is untied money the States may spend as they choose, while grants are often conditional, so a shift from grants to devolution (14th FC) raises the share of unconditional transfers.

50.s: The percentage of distribution of revenue from taxes between the Centre and the States is recommended by the
50.x: The Finance Commission (Art. 280) recommends the sharing of tax revenue between the Centre and the States; NITI Aayog, the Inter-State Council and the NDC have no such role.

50.s: With reference to the Finance Commission of India, which of the following statements is correct?
o: It encourages the inflow of foreign capital for
It facilitates the proper distribution of finances among
It ensures transparency in financial administration
50.x: Under Art. 280(3) the Finance Commission recommends tax devolution, grants-in-aid principles and local-body resources; it does not attract foreign capital, distribute funds among PSUs or ensure transparency in administration, so none of the statements is correct.

50.s: The principles concerning the provisions of the grants-in-aid to the states out of the Consolidated Fund of India are recommended by the
50.x: The principles governing grants-in-aid to States out of the CFI are recommended by the Finance Commission (Art. 280(3)(b)), not the Planning Commission, NDC or ARC.

50.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Sixteenth Finance Commission?
o: It retained the vertical share of States in the divisible pool at 41%
The Union Government accepted this recommendation in Budget 2026–27
Vertical share refers to distribution of the divisible pool among individual States
Distribution of the divisible pool among individual States is inter se devolution
50.x: Vertical devolution concerns the Centre–State share; distribution among individual States is inter se (horizontal) devolution.
xa: Non-shareable cesses (~**18%** of gross tax revenue) cut effective devolution to about **31-32%**.
The **16th FC** caps state fiscal deficit at **3% of GSDP**.

50.s: What was the tax devolution to the States in 2024-25?
50.x: Tax devolution in 2024-25 was Rs 12.87 lakh crore against a Budget Estimate of Rs 12.47 lakh crore.

50.s:
Consider the following statements about the Finance Commission:
1. It is a quasi-judicial body constituted by the President under Article 280 every fifth year or earlier.
2. Under Article 280(3) it recommends both the vertical and the horizontal distribution of the net proceeds of taxes.
3. Because cesses and surcharges stay outside the divisible pool, the effective devolution to States is about 41-42%.
4. The southern States' 'Chalo Delhi' protest of 2024 mainly opposed the tax-effort criterion in devolution.
How many of the above statements are correct?
50.x: Statement 3 is incorrect – since cesses and surcharges (~18% of gross tax) stay outside the pool, effective devolution is only about 31-32%. Statement 4 is incorrect – the 2024 'Chalo Delhi' protest opposed POPULATION-based criteria in devolution. Statements 1 and 2 are correct as per the notes.

50.src: General Overview of the Indian Constitution & Welfare Paper-
50.x: Article 275 provides statutory grants-in-aid from the Union to States in need, charged on the CFI and given on the Finance Commission's advice. Art. 205 is supplementary State grants, 224 additional HC judges and 344 the Official Language Commission.

50.s: Which article of the Constitution states that "No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law"?
50.src: APPSC Hostel Welfare Officer Grade-II Screening Test 2017
50.x: Article 265 says no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law. Art. 266 is the Consolidated Fund and Public Accounts, 267 the Contingency Fund and 264 the interpretation clause of Part XII.

50.s: The Article of the Constitution that provides for the establishment of Union Finance Commission:
50.x: The Finance Commission is constituted by the President under Article 280. Art. 360 is Financial Emergency; 287 and 289 deal with electricity taxes and exemption of State property.

50.s: The financial relations between the Union Government and States have been discussed under –
50.x: Chapter I of Part XII, 'Distribution of Revenues between the Union and the States', runs from Article 268 to Article 281; financial relations as a whole are Arts 268-293.

50.s: Provision for Descretionary Grant which may be given by Central government to States is given under which Article of the Constitution?
50.x: Article 282 lets the Union (or a State) make grants for any public purpose, even outside its legislative field – the discretionary grants. Art. 275 is statutory grants and 281 the laying of the FC report.

50.s: Which of the Constitutional Provision lays down that taxes can neither be levied nor collected without the authority of law?
50.x: Article 265: no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law. Art. 266 deals with the Consolidated Funds, 300 with suits, and 368 with amendment.

50.s: Which Article of Indian Constitution provides the scheme of the distribution of revenue between the Union and the States?
50.src: APPSC Extension Officer in Women & CW 2012
50.x: Part XII Chapter I, 'Distribution of Revenues between the Union and the States', begins at Article 268 (Arts 268-281). Arts 265-267 deal with taxation by law, the Consolidated Fund and the Contingency Fund.

50.s: Who certifies the net proceeds relevant to the divisible pool?
o: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
50.x: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India certifies the net proceeds used in determining the divisible pool.

xs: **Net proceeds** are certified by the **Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)** — option **(4)**.
The FC recommends the sharing; the CAG certifies the proceeds.
xa: Divisible pool = **Art. 270** taxes.
**CAG's State Finances 2023-24** report is in current relevance.

50.s: Which Article exempts the property of the States from Union taxation?
50.x: Article 289 exempts State property from Union taxes, though the Centre can tax a State's commercial operations.

50.s: Which Part of the Constitution deals with Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits?
50.x: Part XII (Articles 264-293) deals with Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits.

50.s: Into which fund are all revenues received by the Union, the loans raised by it and repayments of its loans credited?
50.x: Under Article 266, all Union revenues, loans raised and loan repayments go into the Consolidated Fund of India.

50.s: Which of the following tax is not subsumed by the Goods And Services Tax recently introduced in India?
50.src: APPSC Group-III Panchayat Secretary Mains Paper-I General St
50.x:
Most keys: Land Revenue. Strictly, State excise on alcoholic liquor for human consumption is also not subsumed in GST (liquor is outside GST, Art. 366(12A)), so option 1 is also right.
Land revenue is a direct State tax on land and was never part of GST, while entry tax and entertainment tax (other than by local bodies) were subsumed. State excise on alcohol for human consumption was also kept out of GST, so the stem is loose; land revenue is the better answer.

50.s: What monetary limit has been recommended by the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council meeting held in June 2024 for filing appeals under GST by the department before the Supreme Court of India to reduce government litigation?
50.src: APPSC Junior Assistant in Dr. NTR University of Health Scien
50.x: The 53rd GST Council (22 June 2024) set monetary limits for departmental appeals of ₹20 lakh before the GSTAT, ₹1 crore before High Courts and ₹2 crore before the Supreme Court.

o: Enables States to be equal partners with Centre on tax matters
Pushes States to a secondary role in tax matters
Does not alter the existing relations
Enables Centre and States to act independently
50.src: APPSC Asst. Social, BC & Tribal Welfare Officers Screening T
50.x: GST rests on 'pooled sovereignty': the Centre and the States decide GST jointly in the GST Council (Art. 279A), so the States act as partners with the Centre rather than independently or in a secondary role; it clearly alters the earlier relations.

50.x: The GST Council (Art. 279A) is chaired by the Union Finance Minister; the Union MoS (Revenue/Finance) and State Finance Ministers are members.

o: The Constitutions (One Hundred and First) Amendment

50.x: GST, in force from 1 July 2017, replaced about 17 indirect taxes.

3. GST is an origin-based tax.

50.x: Statement 3 is incorrect – GST is DESTINATION-based. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct as per the notes.

50.s:
Assertion (A): IGST revenue on an inter-State supply goes to the destination State.
Reason (R): Under Article 246A, only Parliament can make GST laws on inter-State supply.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
50.x: Both are true: Art. 269A sends IGST revenue to the destination State, and Art. 246A gives Parliament alone the power over inter-State supply. But who makes the law does not explain where the revenue goes – R does not explain A.

50.s:
Consider the following statements about the GST Council:
1. A decision requires two-thirds of the weighted votes of the members present and voting.
2. Its members are the Union Finance Minister, the Union Minister of State for Revenue/Finance and the Finance Minister of every State.
3. In Mohit Minerals (2022) the Supreme Court held its recommendations binding on Parliament and the State Legislatures.
4. The vote of the Centre carries a weight of one-third of the total votes cast.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
50.x: Statement 1 is incorrect – a decision needs THREE-FOURTHS of the weighted votes, so neither side can carry it alone. Statement 3 is incorrect – Mohit Minerals held them persuasive, NOT binding. Statements 2 and 4 are correct as per the notes.

50.s:
Consider the following statements:

2. 'GST 2.0' took effect from September 2024.

o: separate representation in the Finance Commission
transfer of all Union taxes to the State

50.s:

50.s: Is a State of the Indian Union empowered under the Constitution to take foreign loans directly?
o: Yes, but from international organizations only

50.s: What did the Article 131 suit in Kerala v. Union of India (2024) challenge?

The validity of GST under Article 279A

50.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the 80th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000?
o: It gave effect to the Tenth Finance Commission's 'Alternative Scheme of Devolution'

55.x:

Some guides (gktoday.in) list 'use Art. 356 only in a complete breakdown of law and order' as its recommendation – on that reading every printed option is a recommendation. The Rajamannar Committee (TN, 1969-71) wanted an Inter-State Council set up at once, with Bills and decisions of national importance referred to it, and residuary powers of legislation and taxation vested in the States. The printed key (residuary powers to States) was in fact one of its recommendations.

The returned candidate was not qualified
The returned candidate won by a very small margin

64.s: VVPAT slips must be counted in which of the following circumstances?
o: Whenever EVM data and Form 17C do not match
Whenever postal ballots exceed the number of EVM votes
Only in constituencies using postal ballots
Only when the winning candidate requests it after the declaration of results

APPSC Group-II 2011 key: 25 years (21 was not offered). Strictly: 21 years (Art. 243V; Laxmikanth 8th ed. ch.40 p.122).
Art. 243V: no person is disqualified for being under 25 if he/she has attained 21, so the minimum age for a municipal member is 21. 25 (the printed key) is the Assembly age, not the municipal one; 30, 35 and 40 are other offices' ages.

82.s:

2. One-third of the total number of seats to be filled by direct election in the municipalities is reserved for women.
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
82.x: Statement 1 is wrong – the qualifying age is 21 (Art. 243V), not 25. Statement 2 is right – at least one-third of directly elected seats are reserved for women (243T). So only 2.

82.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about reservation for women in local bodies?

n: Article 243D deals with reservations in Panchayats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 94-97]
Article 243T deals with reservations in Municipalities. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 94-97]

xa: Composition: **243C** / **243R**, regulated by the **State Legislature**; minimum age **21** years.
**243G / 243W**: economic development, social justice, sanitation, public health.

82.s: Which one of the following is NOT a compulsory provision under the 74th Amendment?
o: Reservation for backward classes in every municipality
Ward Committees in municipalities having a population of three lakh or more
Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to population
82.x: Reservation for backward classes is voluntary and is left to the State legislature. Ward Committees for municipalities with a population of three lakh or more, five-year terms, and SC/ST reservation are compulsory provisions.
82.tq: Find the provision expressly left to State legislative discretion among otherwise mandatory features.
xs: **Reservation for backward classes** is **voluntary** — option **(1)**.
Compulsory: **Ward Committees** (**3 lakh or more**), **SC/ST reservation** by population, **5-year** term.
xa: Other voluntary items: representation of **MPs, MLAs, MLCs**; manner of electing the **Chairperson**.
Devolving the Twelfth Schedule subjects (**243W**) is also voluntary.

82.s:
Consider the following statements about the composition of municipalities (Article 243R):
1. All members of a municipality are directly elected from territorial constituencies called wards.
2. Persons with special knowledge or experience in municipal administration may be represented with the right to vote in meetings.
3. The manner of electing the chairperson is left to the State Legislature.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
82.x: Statement 2 is wrong: persons with municipal-administration experience may be represented, but WITHOUT the right to vote. Members are directly elected from wards; the chairperson's election is left to State law.

82.s:
Consider the following statements about municipalities:
1. The term is five years from the date appointed for the first meeting.
2. A municipality must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before dissolution.
3. An election must be held within one year of dissolution.
4. Disqualifications are mainly as under the law for elections to the State Legislature.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
82.x: Statement 3 is wrong: a fresh election must be completed within six months of dissolution (243U). The term is five years from the first meeting; disqualifications follow the State Legislature election law or a State law (243V).

82.s:
Consider the following:
Assertion (A): A 22-year-old is disqualified from being a member of a municipality because he is under 25.
Reason (R): Article 243V fixes the minimum age for membership of a municipality at 21 years.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
82.x: A is false, R is true: no one is disqualified for being under 25 if he or she is 21 - the constitutional minimum age (243V; 243F for Panchayats) is 21.

82.s: Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils and Nagar Panchayats are three types of ___ local Governments.
82.src: AP Grama Ward Sachivalayam Ward Welfare & Development Secret
82.x: Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils and Nagar Panchayats are the three types of municipalities under Art. 243Q – urban local governments; rural bodies are Panchayats.

82.x: Art. 243Q: a Nagar Panchayat is constituted for a transitional area – one in transition from rural to urban; a Municipal Council is for a smaller urban area.

82.s: Twelfth Schedule of the Indian Constitution contains ____ functional items.
82.x: The Twelfth Schedule (74th Amendment) lists 18 functional items of municipalities.

82.s:
Assertion (A): The Twelfth Schedule includes functions relating to urban poverty alleviation.
Reason (R): The Twelfth Schedule is concerned exclusively with physical infrastructure such as roads, bridges and water supply.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
82.x: The Assertion is true because urban poverty alleviation is a Twelfth Schedule subject. The Reason is false because the Schedule also covers social, environmental, cultural and regulatory functions, not exclusively physical infrastructure.
82.tq: Test the absolute word “exclusively” in the Reason against the wider range of municipal functions.
xs: **A is true but R is false** — option **(3)**.
A true: **urban poverty alleviation** is a **Twelfth Schedule** item.
R false: the Schedule also covers **welfare**, **health and environment**, **culture** and civic items — not only roads, bridges and water supply.
xa: Welfare items: **weaker sections** incl. disabled; **slum improvement and upgradation**.
Civic items: **vital statistics**, **cattle pounds**, **slaughter houses and tanneries**.
The Twelfth Schedule has **18** items, linked to **Art. 243W**.

n: Article 243J deals with accounts and audit of Panchayats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 94-97]

The State Legislature provides for the audit of accounts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 94-97]

Under **Article 243J**, the **State Legislature** provides for maintenance and **audit** of Panchayat accounts.

82.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Establishment of the first Municipal Corporation at Madras
B. Lord Ripon’s Resolution on Local Self-Government
C. Local Self-Government becoming a Transferred Subject under the Government of India Act
D. Introduction of Panchayati Raj in Rajasthan
82.x: The Madras Corporation came first (1688), then Ripon's Resolution (1882), the 1919 Act and Rajasthan's Panchayati Raj (1959). The order is A, B, C, D.
n: Lord Ripon’s 1882 Resolution recognized Lord Ripon as the Father of Local Self-Government in India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 94-97]
The Government of India Act, 1919 made Local Self-Government a Transferred Subject under provincial dyarchy. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 94-97]
Rajasthan was the first Panchayati Raj State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 94-97]
The first Panchayati Raj system in Rajasthan was established in Nagaur District. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 94-97]
The first Panchayati Raj system was established in Rajasthan on 2 October 1959. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 94-97]
Madras established the first Municipal Corporation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 94-97]
The first Municipal Corporation was established in Madras in 1688. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 94-97]
xs: Correct order: **A, B, C, D** — option **(1)**.
**Madras** Municipal Corporation (**1688**) → **Lord Ripon's Resolution** (**1882**) → **GoI Act, 1919** (Transferred Subject) → **Panchayati Raj in Rajasthan** (**2 October 1959**).
xa: **Bombay** and **Calcutta** corporations followed Madras in **1726**.
**Lord Mayo's** resolution on financial decentralisation came in **1870**.
UP set up corporations in the five **KAVAL towns** (**1953**); UP Municipal Corporations Act **1959**.
**Andhra Pradesh** was the **second** Panchayati Raj state.

85.s:
Consider the following statements about public policy:

85.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the Right to Food was read into Article 21 – an example of judicial interpretation as a basis of policy. Statements 1 and 3 are correct.

85.s: Which of the following is a remedy, not a cause, of policy failure?
85.x: Real-time outcome tracking is a remedy; weak coordination, poor targeting and resource shortfalls cause policy failure.

ii. PLI incentives

85.x: Taxes and subsidies – PLI incentives, DBT subsidy reform; direct provision – schools, PHCs; information – RTI s.4 disclosure, campaigns; nudges – Thaler and Sunstein.

85.s:
Consider the following statements about policy instruments and implementation:

3. The concept of 'street-level bureaucracy' was given by Richard Elmore.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
85.x: Statement 3 is wrong: street-level bureaucracy (1980) is Michael Lipsky's; Elmore is associated with backward mapping. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

85.s:
Assertion (A): The bottom-up approach to implementation stresses the role of front-line officials in shaping policy outcomes.
Reason (R): 'Backward mapping' was proposed by Pressman and Wildavsky.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
85.x: A is true – Lipsky's street-level bureaucracy is the classic bottom-up view. R is false: backward mapping is Richard Elmore's idea; Pressman and Wildavsky wrote the top-down study 'Implementation'.

85.s:
Assertion (A): Nudges as a policy instrument rely on behavioural design.
Reason (R): Hood's NATO tools of government are Nodality, Authority, Treasure and Organisation.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
85.x: Both are true, but R does not explain A: nudges come from Thaler and Sunstein's behavioural design, while NATO is Hood's separate classification of tools.
